item.title: Reflections on an Essay by Wigner | Sergiu Klainerman | Inference
item.description: Eugene Wigner famously pondered why so many mathematical concepts turn out to play such a fundamental role in physics. In this essay, Sergiu Klainerman retraces the development of modern mathematics, unexpected consequences in physics, and the perennial question of whether mathematics is itself a science.

item.title: Counting in the Dark | Partha Ghose | Inference
item.description: Born in 1894, Satyendra Nath Bose was one of the leading luminaries of twentieth century physics. Written by Bose’s former student, Partha Ghose, this account pays tribute to the life of a trailblazer who, along with Albert Einstein, established a new direction in quantum mechanics, and whose name will echo in the annals of scientific discovery for centuries to come.

item.title: When Existence is Inefficient | Allyn Jackson | Inference
item.description: How hard is it to solve a problem when a solution is guaranteed to exist? It is to address questions like this that the theoretical computer scientist Christos Papadimitriou invented the complexity class PPAD. Allyn Jackson explores the origins and impact of PPAD, and how it differs from the complexity class NP.

item.title: The Scent of Flavor | Linda Bartoshuk | Inference
item.description: Had Aristotle recognized flavor as a sensation distinct from taste, he might have paid attention to how taste, flavor, and smell really work together. It was, in fact, only in the nineteenth century that this distinction was realized. Linda Bartoshuk retraces the history of our understanding of flavor, and recounts tales from her life’s work researching the chemical senses of taste and smell.

item.title: The Origins of Python | Lambert Meertens | Inference
item.description: Python is arguably the most popular programming language worldwide. Since its debut in 1991, Python’s accessibility and rich functionality has helped it gather a huge userbase. Its design was influenced by creator Guido van Rossum’s involvement with an earlier language, ABC. Lambert Meertens, one of ABC’s developers, recounts Python’s origins and how ABC’s design philosophy shaped its successor.

item.title: The Chinese Civil Examinations | Hilde De Weerdt | Inference
item.description: From the end of the sixth century onwards the written civil service examinations became a staple of life in Imperial China. These examinations were used, among other things, to assign positions in political office, and thus to reduce the power of aristocratic families. Hilde de Weerdt examines the rise of the civil service examination, and reassesses its promise of social mobility.

item.title: Planetary Intelligence | Charles Lineweaver | Inference
item.description: Can the idea of intelligence as a collective property be extended to a planetary scale? A recent paper uses this framework to explore possible trajectories for the long-term evolution of inhabited planets, including our own. In his review, Charles Lineweaver is less convinced about such claims and the notion that a mature, sustainable technosphere could be the enduring culmination of our future.

item.title: On the Laser-Fusion Milestone | Daniel Jassby | Inference
item.description: On December 5, 2022, the National Ignition Facility recorded the first energy gain in fusion history. Daniel Jassby follows up on his recent essay in Inference to explain that, while laudable, these results have done little to advance fusion energy’s distant future, since the various technologies necessary to support such a future do not yet exist.

item.title: 2022: The Year in Review | The Editors | Inference
item.description: As the end of the year approaches, the editors are delighted to present our second annual review, highlighting the essays that best represent our aims, ambitions, attitudes, and even our animadversions. Collected here are some notable essays we published this year, some illuminating exchanges from our letters section, and a selection of our favorite links from The Rambler.

item.title: A Truncated Manuscript | Pierre Schapira | Inference
item.description: In the mid-1980s, an enigmatic document began circulating in French mathematical circles. Entitled Récoltes et Semailles, it was a lengthy, philosophical and deeply personal tract from the elusive mathematician Alexander Grothendieck, by then living in self-imposed seclusion. Now published officially for the first time, Pierre Schapira casts a critical eye over the book and some notable omissions.
